A lodger is a person who pays money (rent) to live in a room inside someone else's home — while the owner of that home also lives there at the same time.

That last part is the heart of the word. The owner doesn't move out. Both people — the owner and the lodger — share the same house or flat. The lodger typically has their own bedroom (sometimes their own bathroom too), but they usually share common areas like the kitchen, hallway, or living room with the owner.

Imagine a woman named Sarah. She owns a three-bedroom house but lives alone. One bedroom sits empty. To earn extra money, she rents that spare room to a man named Tom. Tom pays Sarah a fixed amount every month, and he lives in that room. He uses her kitchen to cook, passes her in the hallway, and shares her home — but Sarah is still there, living her own life in the same house.

Tom, in this situation, is Sarah's lodger.
What makes a lodger different from a tenant?

This distinction matters, and learners often confuse the two.

A tenant rents an entire property — a whole flat or house — that belongs to someone else. The owner (landlord) does not live there. The tenant has the place to themselves and typically has strong legal rights over that space. They have what's called a tenancy agreement.

A lodger, on the other hand, rents just a room within the owner's own home. The owner does live there. A lodger has a licence to occupy — a more informal, less legally protected arrangement than a tenancy. This means the owner has considerably more power to ask a lodger to leave (usually with shorter notice) than they would have with a formal tenant.

In short:

  • Tenant → rents the whole place → owner lives elsewhere → stronger legal rights
  • Lodger → rents one room → owner lives in the same home → weaker legal protections

Because a lodger lives inside the owner's home, the arrangement is naturally more personal and domestic than a standard rental. Some owners cook meals for their lodger or include meals in the rent — though this is not required. The shared spaces (kitchen, bathroom, etc.) are agreed upon between the two parties.

The owner of the home in this arrangement is sometimes called the landlord (if male) or landlady (if female), but in the context of lodging, you might also hear them called the host informally, since they are essentially hosting someone in their private home.
Why do people take in lodgers, and why do people become lodgers?

People take in lodgers (i.e., become the hosting owner) mainly to earn extra income from a spare room — for example, to help pay their mortgage or bills.

People become lodgers typically because it is cheaper than renting a whole flat, because they need a place to stay for a limited time, or because they prefer a more home-like environment rather than a commercial apartment complex.

In many countries — especially the United Kingdom, where the word "lodger" is most commonly used — there are specific legal rules around lodgers. Because the owner lives in the same property, they retain the right to enter the lodger's room (with reasonable notice) and can typically end the arrangement more quickly than a landlord could evict a formal tenant. A lodger does not have the same security of tenure (the legal right to stay) as a tenant does.

This is why, legally and practically, the word "lodger" signals a specific type of living arrangement — not just "someone who pays rent to live somewhere."

The word "lodger" is used most naturally and commonly in British English. If you're reading a British novel, newspaper, or legal document, you will encounter it regularly. In American English, the concept exists but people are more likely to say boarder (especially historically, or when meals are included) or simply renter. However, "lodger" is understood in American English too.

The word is fairly neutral in register — it works in everyday conversation, legal documents, and formal writing alike.

• To lodge (verb): To live somewhere temporarily, or to rent a room in someone's house. Example: "He lodged with a retired teacher during his studies."
  • Lodgings (noun, usually plural): A rented room or set of rooms in someone's house where you pay to live. Example: "She found lodgings near the university."
  • Lodging house (noun): A house where multiple rooms are rented out to lodgers.

• "The family decided to take in a lodger after their youngest child moved out."
  • "As a lodger, he had his own room but shared the bathroom with the owner."
  • "She placed an advertisement for a lodger to help cover the rent on her flat."
  • "Unlike a tenant, a lodger has fewer legal protections because the owner lives on the premises."
  • "He was a quiet, considerate lodger who never caused any trouble."

A lodger is someone who rents a room in another person's occupied home — the owner lives there too. The lodger pays rent, typically has their own bedroom, and shares parts of the house with the owner. The arrangement is more personal and legally informal than a full tenancy. The word is especially common in British English and carries a specific legal meaning: a lodger has a licence to occupy a room, not a tenancy over an entire property.
